newsitem.title: CHINA: HK's Patten stirs up democracy storm from afar.
newsitem.headline: HK's Patten stirs up democracy storm from afar.

text.p: Like a voice from the grave, last British governor Chris Patten leaped back into Hong Kong politics from afar on Monday with accusations that Britain had delayed democracy here in order to appease China.
Martin Lee, leader of Hong Kong's pro-democracy camp who was ousted from the legislature after last week's handover to China, seized upon Patten's allegations and demanded a public inquiry.

Analysts said Patten's remarks, published less than a week after his departure from Britain's ex-colony, could spark a furious debate over who was really to blame for China's move to slash democracy and civil rights here after the change of flag.
Beijing took back the territory on July 1 after 156 years of British colonial rule and scrapped its elected legislature in order to reverse Patten's expansion of democracy since 1992.

Patten's charges, contained in a book to be published this week, said Britain twisted Hong Kong people's views on a plan for greater democracy in 1988, in a bow to Chinese demands for a delay in direct elections.
Extracts of the book appeared in the Sunday Times newspaper.

It raised questions about the role of former British foreign secretary Sir Geoffrey Howe and ex-ambassador to Beijing Sir Percy Cradock, who were both involved in Hong Kong handover negotiations with China.
Lee said the documents showing Britain deferred introducing democratic elections in Hong Kong before Patten's arrival to avoid upsetting China should be turned over to the public.
"I think the documents should be certainly given to the Foreign Affairs Committee," Lee, widely considered to be the voice of democracy in Hong Kong, told reporters.

"I don't know why he did not expose these secret deals before," Lee said. "It is just too late. Now it is after the event. So when he could have made a difference by revealing these secrets, for whatever reasons he chose not to."

The author of the "The Last Governor", Jonathan Dimbleby, says that in 1987 London advised Beijing to ensure its Hong Kong supporters individually signed statements calling on Britain not to introduce direct elections for a small number of Legislative Council members the following year.

People backing the direct elections proposal signed petitions in large numbers. The Hong Kong government then declared that although the petitions were signed by 230,000 people and the individual statements by just 135,000, more forms had been received against direct elections than in favour.
Patten, credited with making Hong Kong more democratic in his five years as governor, apparently did not know about this "gentleman's agreement", if it existed, when he took office.
He is quoted as saying: "There is absolutely no doubt at all that the majority wanted direct elections."
"If I were a citizen of Hong Kong, I would regard it as very bad that I hadn't been kept in the know and that my views had been treated in this way," Dimbleby quoted him as saying.
He criticised the judgement of Howe and advisers, who at one time included China expert Cradock.
Cradock told Hong Kong radio the book was "shockingly biased", adding: "A full inquiry would be a great blessing. There was no collusive understanding as people are trying to make out."
He said nothing affecting Hong Kong's future could have been achieved without Beijing agreeing and that British negotiators in fact secured a deal for a "a rising curve" of democracy here.
Analyst Joseph Cheng at Hong Kong's City University said evidence pointed to Patten's allegations being true. "I think this is an honest statement from the former governor," he said.

He said the British administration "treated the more than 230,000 signatures collected by the pro-democracy movement in support of direct elections in 1988 as just one submission, so as to draw the conclusion that those who opposed in fact outnumbered those who supported it".
Paddy Ashdown, leader of Britain's minority Liberal Democrats, also called for a parliamentary inquiry.
